issues.failure_explanation: In the proof of Proposition 2.1, the author asserts that matching the first k moments of the empirical distributions on S and T implies that their moments match for all i in N. This is mathematically false: two distinct discrete distributions on n and k points (with n > k) cannot have identical moments of all orders. The proof relies crucially on this assertion to argue that the elements of T are precisely the roots of the k-th orthogonal polynomial P_k associated with S, and that the Christoffel numbers are uniformly equal to 1/k. In general, the roots of P_k depend on moments up to degree 2k-1, which are not determined by the first k moments, and Gauss quadrature weights for general discrete distributions are not uniform. In addition, the proposition defines a_i and b_j as the 'largest' elements while using ordering conventions (b_0=0, b_{k+1}=\infty) corresponding to ascending order.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must establish valid quantile bounds under k matched moments or strengthen the hypotheses to full Gauss-Markov-Stieltjes quadrature conditions.
issues.overall_effect: Proposition 2.1 and Corollary 2.2 are invalid; the claimed interlacing bounds between the quantiles of S and T (and between the spectra of A and B) are unproved and do not follow from matching k moments.
issues.title: False premise that matching k moments implies matching all moments in interlacing proof
issues.why_classification: Proposition 2.1 is presented as a major general interlacing theorem forming the basis of the quantile estimation framework. Its proof fails fundamentally and no comparable result with uniform weights follows from the source arguments.

issues.failure_explanation: Equation (2.5) requires the integral ratio to equal s + \epsilon for all s in [t, 1], which at s = 1 forces \epsilon = 0. Furthermore, the product in (2.5) is indexed up to l, whereas a walk \pi has length r >= l. In the proof of (2.6), bounding the expectation ratio requires relating \int_{[0, 1/z_1]^l} to (1/z_1) \int_{[0,1]^l}. The lower bound uses (1 - \epsilon)/z_1 <= 1/z_1 + \epsilon, but establishing the upper bound (1 + \epsilon) would require 1/z_1 + \epsilon <= (1 + \epsilon)/z_1, which is equivalent to z_1 <= 1. However, distribution \Xi has E[z_1] = (n-1)/(k-1) > 1 and its support takes values strictly greater than 1 (e.g., up to ~130 in Example 2.1). The error \epsilon is amplified by z_1^l rather than bounded by \epsilon.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must correct condition (2.5) to a valid perturbation bound and rigorously control the error propagation under scaling by z_1 > 1.
issues.overall_effect: Proposition 2.3 fails to guarantee that the expected traces of B^r/k and A^r/n match within relative error 1 \pm \epsilon, undermining the theoretical guarantee of the moment matching scheme.
issues.title: Inconsistent decay condition and unestablished trace expectation upper bound
issues.why_classification: The quantitative moment matching guarantee between the subsampled matrix B and the target matrix A is one of the central formal results of the paper, and its proof cannot deliver the claimed relative accuracy.

issues.failure_explanation: In the proof of Proposition 2.4, the author evaluates \frac{1}{\frac{k}{n}\binom{n}{k}} \mu_l as \frac{(n-k)!(k-l-1)!}{(n-l-1)!} and equates it to (n-k) \int_0^1 x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k-l} dx. However, by the definition of the Beta function, (n-k) \int_0^1 x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k-l} dx = (n-k) \frac{(n-k-1)!(k-l)!}{(n-l)!} = \frac{(n-k)!(k-l)!}{(n-l)!}, which differs from the required quantity by a factor of (k-l)/(n-l) != 1. As a consequence, H_{k,n} is not the Gram matrix of {v_i} in V, and the proof that H_{k,n} and H'_{k,n} are positive definite fails.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Adjust the definition of the functions v_i, w_j and the measure on [0, 1] to correctly represent \mu_l as an inner product, or apply standard moment sequence theorems (such as Hausdorff/Stieltjes moment criteria for completely monotonic sequences) to establish positive definiteness.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Proposition 2.4 does not establish that the Hankel matrices H_{k,n} and H'_{k,n} are positive definite, leaving the general existence of the scaling distribution \Xi unproven.
issues.title: Algebraic error in Beta integral evaluation in Gram matrix construction
issues.why_classification: The error is a localized miscalculation in a Gram matrix representation; the positive definiteness of the Hankel matrices for this hypergeometric moment sequence is an established property that can be resolved without changing the statement or architecture of the paper.
